A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EVA research work despite the changed title. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison, including material relocated between versions.

before.justification: V2 reports original fine-tuning experiments in language generation, language understanding, image classification, and decision making, together with appendix ablations and convergence analyses.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and adds comparator results, gradient-norm measurements, and peak-memory measurements.

M1.justification: Both versions use incremental truncated SVD of downstream activations, right-singular-vector initialization of A, zero initialization of B, and explained-variance-based rank redistribution controlled by rho. The revised explanation and theoretical framing do not change the EVA procedure or its allocation formula.

E1.justification: Both retain the eight commonsense tasks, MetaMathQA with GSM8K/MATH evaluation, Code-Feedback with four coding benchmarks, GLUE, VTAB-1K, and Meta-World MT40/CW10. The added comparisons and diagnostics use existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: CorDA becomes an evaluated comparator for commonsense and math reasoning with three LLMs and for both GLUE models. LoRA-GA also joins the GLUE comparison, and both methods join the Llama-3.1-8B loss comparison. These additions substantially expand comparisons with competing data-driven initializers; the vision, coding, and decision-making comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The newly added CorDA evaluations introduce an initialization-sample search from 256 to 2560 examples, documented in v4 Appendix A.2. Gradient-norm and peak-memory measurements add evaluation procedures. Existing benchmark splits, model configurations, and training budgets remain as documented.

E4.justification: V4 Figure 3 adds a gradient-norm diagnostic to investigate the proposed amplification mechanism, and Table 3 adds memory profiling. The extensive rank, whitening, rotation, permutation, normalization, adapter-distance, and SVD-invariance analyses already present in v2 are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 25 states that training time was averaged over two one-epoch runs; v4 Table 3 omits this repeated-run information. Benchmark seed counts and standard-deviation/standard-error conventions otherwise remain unchanged. Additional comparator rows follow existing reporting practices.

E6.justification: New CorDA and LoRA-GA comparison results, gradient norms, and peak-memory measurements substantially expand the reported outcomes, while retained EVA benchmark means remain unchanged. V4 also replaces the main loss plot with a longer trajectory, removes absolute timing entries, and changes the Gemma-2-9B LoRA-GA GSM8K standard deviation from 0.9 to 0.8 (v2 Table 10; v4 Table 9).

T1.justification: V4 replaces v2's SVD–PCA and data-processing argument with formal variance-optimality and expected-gradient-norm theorems in Sections 3.2–3.3 and rewritten proofs in Appendix G. The gradient proof introduces statistical independence between input activations and the output gradient, an assumption absent from v2's theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift the central theoretical claim from maximizing stored downstream information to provably maximizing the expected gradient signal, including through rank allocation under a fixed budget. This changes the claimed guarantee and contribution, while retaining the broad empirical claims about convergence, performance, and parameter efficiency.

C2.justification: V4 introduces gradient amplification as the main convergence explanation and explicitly discusses high-rank SVD overhead and dependence on a fixed downstream dataset. Appendix I also corrects v2's assertion that methods modifying base weights cannot restore them: restoration can instead use weight differences. CorDA instability receives additional interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 describes a submission archive and planned PEFT integration; v4 reports an existing PEFT implementation and links usage instructions and experiment code. V4 documents CorDA calibration sizes and initialization batch sizes, but drops the earlier LoRA-GA 64-step disclosure and absolute initialization/training times.

R1.justification: Related work shifts its closest-comparator emphasis from AdaLoRA/LoRA-GA to CorDA/LoRA-GA and distinguishes EVA through gradient optimality. CorDA was already cited in v2. References to Beaudry and Renner's data-processing proof and Pearson's PCA work are removed; the broader literature coverage remains largely intact.

P1.justification: The title changes to Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning via Explained Variance Adaptation. The abstract, introduction, method exposition, discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. A separate gradient-signal section is introduced, and supplementary discussions and reproducibility material are reorganized.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn, and the main diagnostic figure combines a new gradient-norm panel with a revised loss plot. Vision and decision-making tables move to the appendix, existing diagnostic panels are regrouped, and the timing table moves into the main text with a memory column replacing absolute-time columns. Typography and layout also change throughout.

improvement.justification: V4 improves comparator coverage, adds useful gradient/memory diagnostics, and clarifies practical limitations and code-access information. However, its newly central gradient-optimality claim exceeds the stated theorem conditions: Appendix G requires input–gradient independence, which Theorem 3.2 omits. Absolute timing and timing-run disclosures are also lost. These empirical and practical gains coexist with claim-support and reproducibility weaknesses, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
